summary:
Thomas Cresap (c.1694–c.1790) was an English-born Maryland settler, trader and land agent whose actions shaped colonial boundary disputes and westward expansion. He emigrated to Maryland at 15 and became an agent for Lord Baltimore in the Maryland–Pennsylvania dispute. Cresap and his men forcibly removed Pennsylvania settlers, making him a central figure in Cresap’s War. Pennsylvania authorities arrested him in 1736; a royal order later forced a boundary settlement against Maryland’s claims.

After his release, Cresap traded along the Potomac and settled near present-day Cumberland. In 1748–1750, he and Delaware leader Nemacolin widened a Native American path into a wagon road toward Redstone on the Monongahela River, creating an important route across the Appalachians. Cresap became a large landowner and raised troops during the French and Indian War. His son Michael later figured in events leading to Lord Dunmore’s War.
